records.title: Aerodynamics
records.description: Aerodynamics as a design consideration that every design shall address (4.2). Generic framework content.
records.guidance: Answer each item for the review stage. A No needs an Action, a Risk or a justification approved by the Discipline Lead (4.5). Items are Draft starter content for review.

items.question: Does the installation affect any external aerodynamic surface?
Are any external protrusions, inlets, outlets or drains identified and their positions agreed?
Are aerodynamic loads on externally exposed items estimated for the flight envelope?
Are external mould line changes, steps and gaps within the agreed aerodynamic tolerances?
Are inlet and outlet flows (vents, drains, cooling air) assessed for effect on drag and local flow?
Are aerodynamic loads provided to Structural Analysis for the preliminary sizing?
Are surface finish, step and gap tolerances on the external surface stated on the drawings?
Are final aerodynamic loads confirmed against the released aerodynamic data set?
Are any items in disturbed flow (for example behind protrusions) assessed for buffet and fatigue?

records.draft_note: Starter checklist items, Draft: to be reviewed with the framework owner before Framework v1.0 release.

records.title: Affordability and Cost
records.description: Affordability and Cost as a design consideration that every design shall address (4.2). Generic framework content.
records.guidance: Answer each item for the review stage. A No needs an Action, a Risk or a justification approved by the Discipline Lead (4.5). Items are Draft starter content for review.

items.question: Is a cost target for the installation set and agreed with the Sub-team?
Are the main cost drivers (bought-in equipment, materials, processes) identified?
Have lower-cost architecture options been considered and the choice recorded?
Is the cost of the installation within the Sub-team allocation?
Are part count and the number of unique parts minimised where practicable?
Are tooling and test equipment costs estimated and included?
Is the final cost estimate within target, or is any overrun recorded as an Issue?
Are standard and common parts used in preference to new made parts where they meet the need?
Are tolerances no tighter than function requires, to avoid unnecessary manufacturing cost?

records.draft_note: Starter checklist items, Draft: to be reviewed with the framework owner before Framework v1.0 release.

records.title: Airworthiness and Certification
records.description: Airworthiness and Certification as a design consideration that every design shall address (4.2). Generic framework content.
records.guidance: Answer each item for the review stage. A No needs an Action, a Risk or a justification approved by the Discipline Lead (4.5). Items are Draft starter content for review.

items.question: Is the applicable certification basis for the installation identified?
Are the certification requirements allocated to the installation listed with a planned means of compliance?
Is the installation's safety and airworthiness significance (Safety Classification) proposed?
Is the means of compliance for each applicable requirement agreed (analysis, test, inspection, similarity)?
Are any novel or unusual design features identified and discussed with the airworthiness authority if needed?
Are certification evidence documents planned with owners and dates?
Is compliance evidence complete, or planned and tracked, for every applicable requirement?
Are Compliance Statements recorded for every inherited and direct Requirement of the FDPS?
Are any non-compliances raised as Issues and visible at release?

records.draft_note: Starter checklist items, Draft: to be reviewed with the framework owner before Framework v1.0 release.

records.title: Assembly, Interfaces, Tolerances and Interchangeability
records.description: Assembly, Interfaces, Tolerances and Interchangeability as a design consideration that every design shall address (4.2). Generic framework content.
records.guidance: Answer each item for the review stage. A No needs an Action, a Risk or a justification approved by the Discipline Lead (4.5). Items are Draft starter content for review.

items.question: Are the installation's physical interfaces with other FDPSs and Systems identified?
Is the build sequence (aircraft Build Station or Bench) proposed for each item?
Are interchangeability or replaceability needs identified?
Is a tolerance stack-up done for each critical interface?
Are datum and location features defined consistently with the mating items?
Can the installation be assembled in the proposed sequence without disturbing other installations?
Are interchangeable items interchangeable at every interface?
Are all interface dimensions and tolerances shown on the released definitions?
Are shimming or fettling allowances defined where tolerance stacks cannot be closed by design?

records.draft_note: Starter checklist items, Draft: to be reviewed with the framework owner before Framework v1.0 release.

items.question: Is the FDPS allocated a number, owning Sub-team and lead Sub-system?

Are changes since the last review recorded as Change Records?
Does the release baseline resolve every member to exactly one revision at every effectivity?
Are superseded definitions and non-interchangeable changes numbered by the roll-by-two rule?
Are all Review Flags on the FDPS dispositioned?

records.title: Pipe-to-structure clearances found late in the design
records.summary: Clearance problems between pipe runs and structure were only found when the full assembly model was checked.
records.what_happened: Pipe routes and structural parts were developed in separate models. When they were combined for a design review, several locations had insufficient clearance once tolerances and pipe movement were included.
records.root_cause: No agreed space-allocation model or regular combined clash check during development; tolerance stack-ups were not included in the clearance criteria.
records.recommendation: Agree space allocation early, run combined clash checks at a set frequency, and define clearance criteria that include tolerances and in-service movement.
records.applicability: Any routed system (fuel, hydraulic, electrical) installed close to structure, from Preliminary Design onwards.

blocks.text: How Requirements are allocated to the System tree and flow to FDPSs. Compliance is claimed once per FDPS, never per part.

Requirements shall be stored as data records and tagged to framework nodes in the Engineering Hub. Requirements shall keep their own levels (2C.7) according to what they are written against. Requirements and TSMs shall flow down to FDPS level only: Parts, Assemblies and items reach their Requirements and TSMs through the FDPS that contains them.

Allocation. Each Requirement shall be allocated to one or more nodes of the System tree: a Sub-system, a System or a System Group. A Requirement shall flow to every FDPS that has at least one Part Instance homed in a Sub-system at or below an allocated node. Example: a Fuel System usable storage requirement is allocated to the Fuel Storage Sub-system, and every FDPS containing a Part Instance homed in Fuel Storage inherits it. A Requirement may also be linked directly to an FDPS, or to an item for traceability, by a Satisfied by link; the FDPS concerned then holds the Requirement directly.
The FDPSs that inherit a Requirement or are directly linked to it shall form the set that must claim compliance against it.

Display and bases. Inherited Requirements and TSMs shall be shown distinctly from directly linked ones. Where a Requirement or TSM reaches an FDPS by several routes (for example directly, and through a Sub-system), every route shall be recorded as a basis of its Compliance Statement.

Non-applicability. An FDPS may record that an inherited Requirement or TSM does not apply, with a reason and approval (6C.13). The inheritance shall not be deleted. For a TSM, a non-applicability record is required only where none of its statements applies to the FDPS (6B.11).

Change flags. A changed Requirement or TSM shall flag the Compliance Statements of every FDPS that inherits it or is directly linked to it. A changed item, revision or Verification shall flag the Compliance Statements whose evidence it affects.

A TSM is a broad document holding many statements. It is tagged with Design Types, Disciplines and Systems, and reaches an FDPS when any one tag matches (OR). Over-tagging is preferred to under-tagging; the designer claims conformance only to the statements that apply.

Technical Standards Manuals (TSMs) shall be a requirement data type: the governing design standards, built from lessons learned and governing body standards (for example those of civil or military airworthiness authorities).

TSM inheritance. Each TSM shall be tagged with one or more of Design Type, Discipline and System. Each kind of tag is optional, but every TSM shall carry at least one tag. A TSM shall reach an FDPS if any one of its tags matches (tags are combined with OR, never AND): a Design Type tag matches when a Part or Assembly in the FDPS's population has that Design Type, including the modification Design Type of a modified bought-in Part (2B.10) and the Design Type Standard Part of catalogue items (1.10.1); a System tag matches when a Part Instance of the FDPS is homed in a Sub-system of that System; and a Discipline tag matches when the Discipline is listed on the Hub page of the FDPS's owning Design Team (the Design Team of its owning Design Sub-team). Matching is never against the Discipline register as a whole, because every Discipline applies to every design (4.2). Where there is doubt, a TSM shall be over-tagged rather than under-tagged. Each Design Team shall list its applicable Design Types and its applicable Disciplines on its Hub page. A Part in an FDPS whose Design Type is not on the owning Design Team's list shall be flagged. Every matching tag is a basis of the Compliance Statement (6B.6).

TSM statements. A TSM is a broad document holding many statements (for example, bonding of fuel system components sits within a Fluid Systems TSM, alongside statements that apply only to hydraulic or pneumatic systems). The Compliance Statement of an FDPS against a TSM shall list the statements of that TSM that apply to the FDPS, and shall claim conformance to those statements only. Each claimed statement may list the Parts to which it applies; listing Parts is optional, and a statement with no Parts listed is claimed for the FDPS as a whole (for example a routing or clearance statement that applies to the installation rather than to a Part). Statements that do not apply need no record, and no non-applicability record is needed for a TSM that applies only in part. The evidence of a Compliant statement shall cover, at each effectivity in its range (6B.9), every listed Part present there for a statement that lists Parts, and the FDPS for a statement claimed for the FDPS as a whole.
One Compliance Statement per FDPS per Requirement or TSM per effectivity range. A Non-compliant statement references its Issue and blocks release over its range.

Compliance Statements. Compliance shall be stated per FDPS per Requirement or TSM, not per Part Instance. Each Compliance Statement shall carry an effectivity range. For any one FDPS and Requirement or TSM, the ranges of its Compliance Statements shall not overlap and shall together cover, with no gaps, the effectivity over which the FDPS's released revisions apply. There shall be one Compliance Statement per FDPS, Requirement or TSM and effectivity range, whatever the number of routes or Part Instances through which the Requirement or TSM reaches the FDPS.

Non-compliance and release. Concessions are part of the manufacturing standard, not the design standard, and Concession records are not in the current scope (section 7). A known non-compliance of the design with a Requirement or TSM shall be recorded as a Compliance Statement with position Non-compliant over the effectivity range concerned, linked to the Issue that records it (2E). No FDPS revision shall be released for any effectivity at which a Compliance Statement of the FDPS is Non-compliant (6C.11). Where a non-compliance is found after a revision has been released, that released revision and its baselines shall stay unchanged as the as-designed record of the effectivities built to it; the Non-compliant statement shall be shown at those effectivities in every view and report (5.17, 2.8), and release for those effectivities shall stay blocked until a Compliance Statement restores compliance. How a built aircraft is recovered or accepted is outside the software until section 7 is in scope.
Each Verification carries its effectivity and the revisions it is based on. Methods come from the Verification method register.

Verification effectivity. Each Verification shall carry the effectivity range over which it is valid evidence. At every effectivity in that range, each of its basis revisions shall be the effective revision of the instances of its definition that exist there. The evidence of a Compliant statement shall cover its range with no gaps. A Verification that supersedes another for the same FDPS and Requirement shall close the range of the one it supersedes, so that their ranges do not overlap.

Verification data shall hold the analysis that supports Product data. Every Verification record shall be linked both to the item(s) it supports and to the Requirement(s) it demonstrates are met, shall state its verification method from the Verification method register (2B.15), and shall carry the effectivity range over which it is valid evidence (6B.9).
Effectivity is held on links, ranges never overlap or leave gaps, and 999 means open-ended. Presence at a selected effectivity is derived, never stored.

Product effectivities. A project shall have multiple product effectivities, identified by project and effectivity number. For example, Project D effectivities 1 to 2 are built to the initial design release standard, and later changes apply to later effectivities.

Effectivity on the link. Effectivity shall be held on the link between a Part Instance (a position) and a Part revision, not on the Part itself. One Part Instance may link to different revisions over different effectivity ranges.

Complete, non-overlapping ranges. For any one Part Instance, the effectivity ranges of its revision links shall not overlap and shall together cover the full effectivity range over which the Part Instance exists (6A.8), with no gaps. The software shall reject or flag any overlap or gap.

Instance effectivity. A Part Instance shall carry its own existence range (instance effectivity), so that Part Instances can be added or removed by effectivity. By default the range is the full effectivity range of the project (for example 1 to 999, 6A.12). Effectivity shall therefore be held on the Part Instance to Part revision link (6A.2) together with the Part Instance's existence range.

Effectivity types. Effectivity numbers shall be the primary effectivity type. Serial ranges and build standards shall be defined as named mappings to effectivity numbers. Each FDPS revision shall carry the effectivity range over which its exact content applies. Releasing a new FDPS revision shall close the range of the previous revision (6A.5, 6A.12), so that the released revisions of an FDPS neither overlap nor leave gaps. The software shall check that the configuration of the FDPS is the same at every effectivity within a revision's range.

Open-ended ranges. An open-ended range shall be written with the placeholder upper value 999 (for example "3 to 999"). The value 999 shall mean "all later effectivities", shall never be allocated as a real effectivity number, and shall be shown as an open-ended range in every view. Closing an open-ended range (6A.5) shall replace 999 with the last effectivity number of that range.

Assembly Instance effectivity. An Assembly Instance shall carry its own existence range (instance effectivity), with the same rules as a Part Instance: effectivity shall be held on the link between the Assembly Instance and its Assembly Definition revision (6A.2); the ranges of those revision links shall not overlap and shall together cover the Assembly Instance's existence range with no gaps (6A.3); by default the existence range is the full effectivity range of the project (6A.8); and open-ended ranges shall follow 6A.12. Assembly Instances shall not themselves be revised (6A.6).

Status for a selected effectivity. Status words shall not imply that an object is out of force when it is only limited by effectivity. The status of a Part Instance, revision or revision link shall be shown for the selected effectivity (Present or Not present, with a note of the ranges over which it applies), and closing a range shall not mark a record as removed.

records.title: Revisions, part numbers and dash numbers

blocks.text: Part numbers are identifiers only. Dash ranges: -001 to -399 made parts, -401 to -799 assemblies, -801 and above FDPSs; odd numbers left-hand or unhanded, even numbers the right-hand version; a non-interchangeable change rolls the dash number by two.
A part number shall be an identifier only. Facet links held as data shall be the master. The software shall never infer a Facet or Category from a part number.

Meaningful part numbers may be retained because they support preliminary design, before links are fully populated. Illustrative example (generic): D2822001-801, read as Project D, System 28 (Fuel, as held in the System code register, 2A.9), Sub-system 2, Major Unit 2, sequence 001, with dash number 801 (an FDPS, 1.11.7).
Meaningful stems suit FDPSs and the parts and assemblies designed for them. Common parts designed by the project (for example common brackets) shall use the lighter convention of 1.11.5.

Stems. FDPS numbers, and the numbers of parts and assemblies designed by the project other than common parts, shall use the meaningful stem of 1.11.2: Project letter, two-digit System code, one-digit Sub-system code, one-digit Major Unit code and three-digit sequence, followed by a three-digit dash number (1.11.7). A part or assembly designed for an FDPS shall take the stem codes of that FDPS (its Project letter, System code, Sub-system code and Major Unit code), with its own sequence number; its own home System, Sub-system and Major Unit are held only in its facet links (1.6), even where they differ from those of the FDPS. A part later used in other FDPSs keeps the stem allocated for the FDPS it was first designed for. The stem shall be fixed when the number is allocated and shall not change if the owned links later change.

Common parts and catalogue items. Only common parts designed by the project shall be numbered Project letter, two-letter Type code and a sequential number (generic example: D-BR-00045, a common bracket). Type codes shall be held in a value register (Annex A.8). Catalogue items (for example fasteners, seals and clamps procured to a standard or from a supplier catalogue) are Standard Parts and shall keep the catalogue number or designation of the standard they are procured to. A change of issue of the standard or catalogue shall be recorded as a revision of the catalogue Part, with an interchangeability assessment (6A.9).

Allocation and uniqueness. The software shall propose a number for each new Part, Assembly and FDPS. The user shall accept the proposed number or propose an alternative. The software shall check every proposed number, whether proposed by the software or by the user, for uniqueness within the project, and shall never allow a number to be reused. The software-proposed number shall be recorded alongside the accepted number, with who proposed and who accepted each, and with every rejected alternative and the reason for its rejection.
Dash numbers. The dash number shall identify the kind of object, from the ranges in Annex B.5: -001 to -399 made parts; -401 to -799 assemblies; -801 and above FDPSs.

Handedness. An odd dash number shall identify a left-hand or unhanded item. The next even dash number shall be reserved for the handed right-hand version of the same item (for example -001 and -002; -401 and -402; -801 and -802), and shall not be used for any other item.

Non-interchangeable change. A change that is not interchangeable in form, fit and function (6A.9) shall keep the stem and roll the dash number by 2 (for example -001 to -003 to -005; -002 to -004 to -006; -401 to -403; -801 to -803). An interchangeable change shall create a new revision and shall never change the dash number (6A.6).

Shared stems and uniqueness. The full number (stem and dash number) shall be unique across FDPSs, assemblies and parts within a project. A stem may be shared to show that items belong together, for example a frame (-001) and the assembly of that frame with a pressed bearing (-401). Distinct items that do not belong together shall take different stems, so that the dash numbers of each stem remain free for handed versions (1.11.8) and non-interchangeable changes (1.11.9).

Bought-in equipment. Bought-in Equipment shall keep the supplier part number, with the supplier's modification standard where one applies, and shall also carry a project control number allocated under 1.11.6. The project control number shall be the Project letter, the code BI and a four-digit sequence (generic example: D-BI-0001), and shall be stored together with the supplier part number. It has no dash number. A bought-in item modified in-house is a new made Part (2B.10) and is numbered under 1.11.4.
Assemblies. Assembly Definitions shall be numbered under the same rules as Parts, and each shall record its numbering scheme.
Up-revision. An up-revision shall close the current effectivity range and open a new one for the new revision.

Terms. Part Definitions, Assembly Definitions and FDPSs shall have revisions; documents shall have issues. Part Instances and Assembly Instances are positions and shall not themselves be revised; changes to a Part Instance are recorded link changes (6A.7). A dash number is part of the part number and shall never be used to indicate a revision.

Interchangeability. A change that keeps a Part interchangeable in form, fit and function in every one of its uses shall create a new revision. A change that does not shall create a new part number, by rolling the dash number under 1.11.9. The software shall record the interchangeability assessment against each change.
A baseline is frozen at each FDPS release and review snapshot; frozen records reference only frozen copies (id@version).

Baselines. A baseline shall be frozen for an FDPS at each FDPS release and at each review snapshot (6C.9). Baselines shall be numbered in sequence within each FDPS revision (for example D2822001-801 rev A, baseline 3). Each baseline shall record the FDPS revision, its effectivity range (6A.11), its population, the revision links and owned links of every member, its Compliance Statements, its interfacing Systems, its FDPS interfaces and the derived views at the time of freezing (for example the Systems of the FDPS and the inferred Categories). A baseline shall point only to frozen copies of records (6A.15), never to live records. Baselines shall never be edited, and the software shall compare any two baselines. The configuration of a product effectivity shall be given by the latest release baselines of the FDPS revisions effective at that effectivity.

Frozen copies. Every saved change to a record shall create a new record version, and earlier versions shall be kept unchanged. Baselines, review snapshots and released FDPS revisions shall reference records by identifier and record version, so that a later change (for example closing the effectivity range of a revision link) never changes what a frozen record shows.

Release master. Until configuration data moves to the Hub (2J.6), the PLM system shall issue revisions and releases, and the Hub shall reflect them. Afterwards the Hub shall issue them and PLM shall synchronise with it.

records.title: Interfaces: lists, inheritance, breaks and FDPS interfaces

blocks.text: Interfaces are set on Sub-system and Sub-structure pages as finite lists. FDPSs inherit them; a break is recorded with a reason and approved by a Design Lead of the FDPS's lead Sub-system. Late decisions applied: R-15 (the lead Sub-system is set by the owning Design Sub-team and approved by a Design Lead of that Sub-system; a change re-runs inheritance and flags breaks for re-confirmation) and R-18 (a cross-FDPS Secures link needs no confirmation; the other FDPS's owner gets a Review Flag and records Accept or Query).

Interface definition. Interfaces shall be defined at Sub-system level, on the Sub-system pages and Sub-structure pages: each page shall list the Systems, or the Sub-systems, with which the items of that Sub-system or Sub-structure interface. Every list shall be finite and decided per System; there shall be no 'interfaces with all' entry. A non-structural Sub-system page shall name the structural Systems or Sub-structures to which its items attach, so that every non-structural FDPS inherits its structural interfaces (R-10). A Sub-structure page shall name the Systems whose items are installed on or attach to that Sub-structure. Interfacing Systems shall be taken from these lists and from Supports links only; they shall not be derived from physical links such as Secures links or geometry (a cross-FDPS Secures link gives an FDPS interface instead, 6C.24). A Sub-structure list may include Systems that some of its FDPSs do not interface with; this over-inclusion is accepted and handled by breaks (6C.21).

Inherited interfacing Systems. An FDPS shall inherit as interfacing Systems: (a) the Systems listed on the Sub-system pages of the non-structural Sub-systems in which its Part Instances are homed; (b) for a Sub-structure FDPS (1.7.7), the Systems listed on the Sub-structure pages of every Sub-structure in which its Part Instances are homed, so that a Sub-structure's list flows down to all the Sub-structure FDPSs in it; and (c) the Systems named in the Supports links of its items. A non-structural FDPS does not inherit the list of a Sub-structure page: its Part Instances homed in a Sub-structure (for example a bracket) contribute only through (c), as before. No inheritance goes beyond what each page lists (R-01). The FDPS's own home Systems are not interfacing Systems. An inherited interface may be broken for an FDPS where it does not apply. Every break shall be approved by a Design Lead whose area is the FDPS's lead Sub-system, or for a Sub-structure FDPS its lead Sub-structure (6C.14), and recorded with its reason, its author, the approver and the date. A broken interface stays visible and shall be flagged for re-confirmation when the FDPS population changes. A change to the interface list of a Sub-system or Sub-structure page shall flag the FDPSs that inherit from it.

Interface agreement. At each review, the position of each interfacing System of the FDPS that is not broken shall be recorded as structured data, with the same positions as Discipline agreement (6C.19), by a person holding a Design Lead role for that System or one of its Sub-systems (6C.14), with the date. Each condition shall be raised as an Action. A Pass shall not be recorded while any required interface position is missing or is Disagree.

Interfaces in snapshots. The review snapshot (6C.9) and the structured difference (6C.18) shall include the FDPS's interfacing Systems, its broken interfaces, its FDPS interfaces (6C.24) and the recorded interface agreements.

FDPS interfaces. Each FDPS shall show its FDPS interfaces, derived from Secures links between its Part Instances and those of other FDPSs (1.6.6), with the other FDPS, the fastener and the held Part Instance. FDPS interfaces shall be included in the review template of each FDPS concerned, for information, and in its snapshots and baselines (6A.10, 6C.23). An FDPS interface is not an interfacing System and needs no interface agreement of its own (6C.22); the interfacing Systems of each FDPS are still set by 6C.21.

Lead Sub-system. Each FDPS shall record exactly one lead Sub-system, which may be a Sub-structure, chosen when the FDPS is created and changed only by a recorded change. At least one Part Instance of the FDPS shall be homed in it once the FDPS is populated; the software shall flag an FDPS for which this is not so. The lead Sub-system sets which Design Lead approves breaks of the FDPS's inherited interfaces (6C.21) and whether the FDPS is a Sub-structure FDPS (6C.21). It does not change the Systems of the FDPS, which are still derived from its Part Instances (1.7.3), and it is not inferred from the FDPS number (1.11.1).

records.title: Design reviews: stages A, B and C

blocks.text: Every FDPS passes three review stages, aligned with Lifecycle Stages 4, 5 and 6. Sign-off team Disciplines listed against a stage give their agreement; Consideration only Disciplines are checked by the designer through the checklist.

Every FDPS shall pass three review stages: A Initial System Design, B Preliminary and C Detail (Scheme Reviews A, B and C). The review stages align with Lifecycle Stages 4 (Initial System Design), 5 (Preliminary Design) and 6 (Detailed Design) respectively (2B.13).
A design review shall cover whole FDPSs. Review documentation shall be linked to every FDPS it covers.
One review may cover several FDPSs. Its template shall be generated from all the FDPSs it covers.

Review content shall include: an introduction, with a structured attendee list giving each person, the Discipline or team represented and the role held, and the review scope; the status of the FDPS's Requirements, with any non-compliances; confirmation of TSMs adhered to, with any non-conformances; agreement from each interfacing System (6C.22); agreement from every Sign-off team Discipline listed against the stage (6C.19); the designer's checklist responses, including the checks of Consideration only Disciplines (4.5); and known risks, held as structured Risk records.
The content required at each stage shall vary as the design matures, and shall be defined in the Engineering Hub.

Each Design Sub-team page shall be split into Initial System Design, Preliminary and Detail stages. Each stage shall list the checklist items to be answered at that stage (4.4), the Sign-off team Disciplines (2B.14) whose agreement is required at that stage and the stage-specific entry criteria (6C.15), and shall link to the relevant guidance and stakeholders. The Requirements, TSMs and interfacing Systems of each FDPS are inferred (6B, 6C.21) and are not listed on the stage page. Together these shall generate the review template for an FDPS at that stage. Design Sub-team stage pages shall be framework templates (generic stage guidance and default item lists) held in the Framework Hub, and shall be tailored for each project in its Production Hub through Tailoring Records (6.4); the tailored pages are production data.
Review material shall be issued to supporting disciplines at least 2 weeks before the review.

Every review shall be minuted. Actions shall be recorded as structured records using the action tracker template and tagged against the FDPSs covered. Each Action shall record who raised it. An Action shall be closed only when its closure evidence has been accepted by the person who raised it or by the review chair; the acceptance shall be recorded with the person and the date.
Each review shall record a snapshot of the relevant design at that point in time, covering content and interfacing Systems, and shall freeze a baseline of each FDPS revision it covers (6A.10).
The exit criterion shall be a Pass or Fail decision by the Technical Authority for Design. Each review shall record its chair.

Discipline agreement. Each Sign-off team Discipline listed against a review stage on the Design Sub-team page (6C.6), other than a Discipline the project has marked not applicable (2B.14), shall record its position before the Technical Authority for Design gives the Pass or Fail decision (6C.10): Agree; Agree with conditions; or Disagree, with reasons. Each condition shall be raised as an Action, to be closed before release (6C.11). The position shall be recorded as structured data on the review, with the person giving it and the date. A Pass shall not be recorded while any required position is missing or is Disagree. Consideration only Disciplines need no agreement at the review; the designer's checklist responses (4.5) are their record.
An FDPS revision is released only after a C pass and with every Action from reviews A, B and C closed and accepted, and with no Non-compliant Compliance Statement over its range.

Release gate. An FDPS revision shall only be submitted to the release lifecycle once the FDPS has passed a C (Detail) review, carried forward where 6C.12 allows, and every Action raised at any A, B or C review covering the FDPS, including re-reviews and Actions raised from conditions of agreement (6C.19, 6C.22), is closed, and every Compliance Statement of the FDPS over the revision's effectivity range is Compliant or an approved Not applicable (6A.17). A Cancelled Action shall count as closed only with a reason and the approval of the review chair. While PLM issues releases (6A.13), the PLM release workflow shall obtain the Hub's confirmation that the gate is met before releasing, through the documented interface (2J.2); a release without that confirmation shall be flagged as a discrepancy.

Carry-forward and re-review. A later design change shall invalidate a review only if it is substantial (6C.17). A passed C review shall carry forward to later revisions of the FDPS unless the Design Authority for the area judges a change since the review snapshot to be substantial. The Design Authority shall assess every change against the snapshot when approving the FDPS revision for release, and the carry-forward shall be recorded with that assessment (assessor, date and reasons). If a change is judged substantial, a re-review shall be held at the FDPS's current review stage (normally C), scoped to the affected FDPS and the changed areas. At a re-review, the agreements required (6C.19, 6C.22) are those of the Disciplines and interfacing Systems whose areas the change affects, as identified by the Design Authority; the other agreements are carried forward from the review it follows and recorded as carried forward. The re-review's snapshot then becomes the reference for later assessments.

Approval of non-applicability. A recorded non-applicability of an inherited Requirement (6B.7) shall be approved by a Design Lead whose delegated area (6C.14) covers every Sub-system through which the Requirement reaches the FDPS. A recorded non-applicability of a TSM (6B.7, 6B.11) shall be approved by a Design Authority whose area covers the FDPS's owning Design Team, or a Design Type through which the TSM reaches the FDPS.

Roles. The Technical Authority for Design (also known as the Design Licence Holder) is responsible for the design and gives the Pass or Fail at each review. The Technical Authority for Design may delegate release authority to Design Leads, Design Approvers or Design Authorities, who approve FDPSs and parts for release within their area. There is no FDPS Design Lead role: breaks of an FDPS's inherited interfaces are approved by a Design Lead whose area is the FDPS's lead Sub-system (1.7.7), which for a Sub-structure FDPS is its lead Sub-structure (6C.21). Each Production Hub shall hold a Role register recording, for each person, each role held (Annex B.4: Technical Authority for Design, Design Authority, Design Lead, Design Approver, Discipline Lead), the delegated authority it carries, the area it covers (for example a Sub-system or Sub-structure, System, Design Sub-team, Design Team, Design Type or Discipline), who delegated it, and its validity dates. The software shall check every approval, agreement, release and decision against the Role register at the date it is given.

Substantial change. A change shall be substantial if, judged against the review snapshot (6C.9), it adversely affects compliance with any Requirement or TSM, degrades form, fit or function, degrades an interface, or adds a new interface with another System. A change that improves or restores compliance does not adversely affect it. A reduced margin that remains compliant shall not count as adversely affecting compliance, but the margin change shall be recorded. Added Part Instances or interfaces shall be substantial only if they add a new interface with another System or adversely affect compliance with a Requirement or TSM. A change that is not substantial shall not require a new review, but shall be recorded against the affected FDPS, with its author, date and reason, and linked to the review it follows. A Change Record may carry several change types, and the substantial assessment shall be recorded for each affected FDPS.

Non-compliance and release. Concessions are part of the manufacturing standard, not the design standard, and Concession records are not in the current scope (section 7). A known non-compliance of the design with a Requirement or TSM shall be recorded as a Compliance Statement with position Non-compliant over the effectivity range concerned, linked to the Issue that records it (2E). No FDPS revision shall be released for any effectivity at which a Compliance Statement of the FDPS is Non-compliant (6C.11). Where a non-compliance is found after a revision has been released, that released revision and its baselines shall stay unchanged as the as-designed record of the effectivities built to it; the Non-compliant statement shall be shown at those effectivities in every view and report (5.17, 2.8), and release for those effectivities shall stay blocked until a Compliance Statement restores compliance. How a built aircraft is recovered or accepted is outside the software until section 7 is in scope.
Every Issue is scored 1 to 5 on five criteria; its escalation level is the highest score, which sets its forum.
The software shall include an Issue data type for recording problems, linked to the Requirements, items and Verification records it affects.

Every Issue shall be assessed against a defined, standard set of impact criteria. Each criterion shall use exhaustive, mutually exclusive options as set out in 2B, worded so that they do not overlap. Where more than one option of a criterion fits an Issue, the highest shall apply.

The software shall determine the escalation level of each Issue from its impact assessment using defined rules, not from the judgement or confidence of the person raising it. An Issue's escalation level shall be its highest score on any single impact criterion.
Each escalation forum or owner shall cover a defined band of escalation levels. The bands shall not overlap and shall together cover every level.
Every Issue shall appear on the agenda of exactly one forum, the one whose band contains its escalation level, whoever raised it. Issues shall be visible read-only to all other forums.
The software shall rank Issues within each forum by impact, so that limited senior attention goes to the highest-impact topics first.
Every Issue page shall show the Product Scopes of the items it links to (and any Product Scope tags on the Issue itself). There shall be no separate cross-scope badge.

Impact criteria. Every Issue shall be scored 1 to 5 on each of the following five criteria: effort, cost, schedule, safety or certification, and scope. Lower limits are exclusive and upper limits inclusive. Threshold values for effort and cost shall be tailorable per Production Hub as project data (6.4); the criteria and scores shall be fixed in the framework.
Escalation bands. The forums and their bands shall be:
Resolution link. An Issue shall be linked to each Change Record that resolves it, by a Resolved by link (2I.2).
One template for every lesson, tagged from the controlled facets and filterable by any combination. Framework lessons are generic; project lessons may be proposed for promotion without project data.
The software shall include a Lessons Learned data type, stored once with a unique, permanent identifier (2A.4).

Every Lesson Learned shall use one standard template: title, summary, what happened, root cause, recommendation, applicability, origin (a source document with its issue or revision and a link, or a data object such as an Issue, by its permanent identifier) and verification status.

Every Lesson Learned shall be tagged from the controlled facets of 2F. Its mandatory tags are at least one Lifecycle Stage and at least one System (or All), per 2F.3 and 2F.12; a lesson without its mandatory tags shall be flagged as invalid.
Users shall be able to filter Lessons Learned by any combination of facets, so that they see all applicable lessons and only applicable lessons.

Promotion to the framework. A project lesson may be proposed for promotion to the framework. It shall first be rewritten in generic form with all project data removed, and shall pass the framework content review (6.10) before it is published as a framework lesson, which may then inform framework Design Considerations and TSMs. The project lesson shall record the framework lesson it was promoted to; the framework lesson shall not reference the project lesson.

The Framework Hub holds only generic, project-independent content and is public. Each Production Hub is a versioned instance of a framework release; project changes to the framework are Tailoring Records. The Demo Production Hub is entirely fictional.
There shall be one standard Engineering Hub framework (the Framework Hub). It defines the page types, templates, controlled facets, link types and generic descriptions that every project uses.

Framework data is the project-independent content of the Framework Hub: the controlled facets and their options (2B, 2F), page templates (5.2), generic page descriptions (5.8), link types (2I.2), schemas (2A.1), and generic guidance and lessons learned that apply to any project. Framework data shall contain no project data.

Production data is the project-specific working data of one project: for example points of contact, project statistics, live views of the product models, part models, calculation documents, project lessons learned, configuration and effectivity records, and the project's tailoring of the framework (6.4).

A Production Hub is a versioned instance of the Framework Hub, created from a numbered framework version and tailored to the project it serves. Tailoring (for example a project's added facet options, page additions or hidden sections) shall be stored as separate project data that references the framework version and the framework page identifiers it modifies; framework pages shall never be edited in a Production Hub. Rationale: keeps framework content stored once (0.3) and lets framework updates be applied without losing tailoring.

Production data shall link to framework pages through the same controlled facets (2F) and by referencing framework page identifiers (2A.4). Framework pages shall never contain or embed production data; a Production Hub shall display the production data linked to each framework page alongside that page. The Production data links table shall include a Requirement column showing the permanent identifier and short title of each Requirement the record supports, as a click-through link.

Production Hub mastery. A Production Hub shall become master of the project's production data data type by data type, as recorded in its authority register (2J). Until a data type has moved, its current master (for example a PLM or CAD system, or released documents) remains authoritative and the Hub holds a typed production link to each record with its identifier and revision or issue.

Configuration control and effectivity. The Production Hub shall manage configuration control and effectivity for the production data it stores or links to: each production record shall carry its revision or issue, the baseline(s) it belongs to, and its applicability (effectivity). Effectivity shall be structured, not free text: a type, a from value, a to value (the placeholder upper value 999 for an open-ended range, 6A.12), and optional notes. Effectivity shall be filterable (for example all records effective for a given effectivity number). Until configuration and effectivity have moved to the Hub (2J), the Hub shall reflect the effectivity set by their current master; afterwards the Hub is master and the integrated tools synchronise with it. The Hub shall show which revision and effectivity apply in each view, including image views of the product (5.10). The detailed configuration control model is set out in 6A.
When a linked production record is superseded or its effectivity changes, the Production Hub shall flag the linked pages and data objects for review, following the link-type table (2I.2).

Framework updates. Updates to the Framework Hub shall be released as numbered framework versions. Each Production Hub shall record the framework version it uses, and shall be able to adopt a newer version in a controlled way: the changes shall be shown, the project's tailoring (6.4) shall be preserved, conflicts shall be flagged for human decision, and adoption shall require human approval.

Security. The Framework Hub shall be hosted publicly. Production Hubs shall be hosted on internal, access-controlled infrastructure, and production data shall never be placed in the Framework Hub. Before each framework version is published, its owner shall complete a content review confirming that it contains no project data or sensitive information.
Framework merge rules. When a Production Hub adopts a new framework version:

records.title: Part attributes: Design Type, Source, Safety Classification, Item Property

blocks.text: Design Type, Safety Classification and Item Property are Part attributes and filters, not trees. Source is a cross-cutting facet.

Product scope, location, function and source shall be separate dimensions, each recorded as its own facet. The kind of design work is recorded as the Design Type attribute of a Part (1.10), not as a facet.

Modified bought-in items. A bought-in item that is modified in-house shall be recorded as a new Part with Source Make, and shall carry a Derived from link (2I.2) to the bought-in source Part. A change to the source Part shall flag the modified Part for review. A modified bought-in Part shall keep the Design Type Bought-in Equipment, and with it the TSMs of that Design Type, and shall also record the Design Type of the modification (for example Metallic - Machined), whose TSMs it shall also bring to its FDPS (6B.5).

Design Type (the kind of design work, for example a material or process kind) shall be an attribute of every Part, with its permitted values held in a value register. Catalogue items (Source Standard Part) shall take the Design Type Standard Part, so that they reach the TSMs tagged with it (6B.5).

Safety Classification shall be an attribute of a Part, with its permitted values held in a value register. A Part used in several places (for example a standard fastener) shall take the highest Safety Classification required by any of its uses. The software shall flag a Part whose classification is lower than that required by any use, for reassignment by a person (0.5).

Property values. Item properties under 4.1 shall be recorded as structured attributes of the Part, drawn from a value register, and may be used to filter considerations and checklists. The item property Fastener shall mark the Parts whose Part Instances require a Secures link (1.6.6). The software shall flag any Part Instance of a Fastener Part that has no Secures link, and any Part Instance with a Secures link whose Part is not a Fastener Part.

Terms used with these meanings throughout (Requirements v23 0.4 and 1.1).

glossary.definition: anything stored in the software with a unique, permanent identifier (2A.4). Every item, record and page is a data object.
the kind of data object, defining its schema (2A.1), for example Requirement, Part Definition, Part Instance, FDPS, Verification, Issue, Lesson Learned, Finish Specification, Hub page.

a physical product item, meaning a Part Instance or an Assembly Instance (1.8). Each Part Instance owns exactly one Build Station link and one Sub-system link; the item directly below the FDPS links to an aircraft Build Station, and a Part Instance within an Assembly Instance links to a Bench Build Station (1.6).
Part Definitions, Assembly Definitions and items together.

a data object that is not an item, for example a Requirement, Verification, Issue, Lesson Learned or Finish Specification. Knowledge records (pages, lessons, issues and requirements) may take several options per facet (2F.3). A production record is a record holding project production data (6.3).
a Hub page (section 5), a data object that presents knowledge and links to other data objects.

glossary.term: Facet, Category, Level, Register, Type, Link, Mapping level, Hub level and Product level
glossary.definition: as defined in 1.1. Option: a Category of a Facet.
the position of a Facet in a tree (1.1 Level). Product Scope is facet level 0. Major Unit and System are alternative splits at facet level 1 (1.3).
a level within one facet that has two tiers, for example System Group (upper tier) and System (lower tier) of the System facet.
the controlled type of a link between data objects, which sets the direction and depth of change flags (2I.2).
a released installation design package of Part Instances, owned by one Design Sub-team (1.7).

a set of parts assembled off-aircraft before installation (1.8). An Assembly Definition defines an assembly once; an Assembly Instance is a single occurrence of it on the product, in the same way as a Part Definition and a Part Instance.
a controlled change state of a Part Definition, Assembly Definition or FDPS (6A.6).
a controlled change state of a document (6A.6). Not to be confused with the Issue data type (2E).
the range of product effectivity numbers for which a link, Part Instance, FDPS revision, Compliance Statement or Verification applies (6A).
a frozen, read-only record of the configuration of one FDPS revision, taken at each FDPS release and at each review snapshot (6A.10).
Technical Standards Manual, a requirement data type holding governing design standards (6B.4). A TSM is a broad document holding many statements (6B.11).
a System of the Airframe System Group (Primary Structure; Secondary Structure; Skins, Doors & Panels; Windscreen & Canopy). Structure means the structural Systems.

a Sub-system of a structural System (2B.11). Sub-structures are the sections into which Structure is split; each Sub-structure page lists its interfacing Systems (6C.20). Sub-system, used alone, includes Sub-structures unless the text says non-structural.

the one Sub-system or Sub-structure recorded on an FDPS that sets which Design Lead approves breaks of its inherited interfaces (1.7.7). A Sub-structure FDPS is an FDPS whose lead Sub-system is a Sub-structure; any other FDPS is a non-structural FDPS.
an interface between two FDPSs, created by a Secures link from a fastener in one FDPS to a Part Instance in the other (1.6.6, 6C.24).
the record of one FDPS's compliance position against one Requirement or TSM over one effectivity range (6B.8).
a System with which an FDPS interfaces, inherited from the interface lists of the Sub-system and Sub-structure pages that apply to it and from the Supports links of its items (6C.20, 6C.21).

a Compliance Statement with position Non-compliant (6A.17). Concession records, Retrofit records and as-embodied or as-manufactured configuration belong to the manufacturing standard and are not in the current scope (section 7).
the record of which person holds which role, with what delegated authority, for which area (6C.14).
one position in a tree, counted from the top node (Full Aircraft). Each level holds nodes of one kind only (for example every node at a given level of the System tree is a System).
one node at a level, into which data is classified. For example, Fuel is a Category at the System level. The Categories at a level are the options of that level's Facet.
a controlled list held in the software. There are two kinds, and they shall be kept distinct:
the kind of a data object, which sets its schema (for example Part, Part Instance, FDPS or Requirement). Type is distinct from the Design Type attribute (1.10).
a typed, directed relationship between two data objects, with a defined cardinality (one-to-one, many-to-one or many-to-many). Links are drawn from the controlled link types (2I.2).

a classification dimension whose permitted values (Categories) are held in a value register. Each Facet sits at one level of one tree, or is cross-cutting (applying at every level, for example Lifecycle Stage).

the level at which a Part Instance is linked to a tree (Build Station in the Manufacturing tree, Sub-system in the System tree, and FDPS in the Design tree). The Categories at all higher levels are inferred from that link and are not stored again.
a tree level that exists as Hub pages. Hub levels form the control framework and carry guidance, ownership, metadata and live model previews (5.16).
a tree level that exists as product data records (for example Part and Part Instance). Product levels are not Hub pages.

blocks.text: How people get access to a Production Hub: Users, named access roles per project, effectivity restrictions, one-off permission overrides, and one accountable Owner with optional Contributors on every work item. Access roles are separate from the authority (approval) roles of the Role register. Clauses quoted from Requirements Prompt v24.6, section 5A and Annex B.6 (confirmed by Daniel, 12 Oct 2026).

Users. Every person who uses a Production Hub shall be a User record with a permanent identifier, name, email, Design Team and Design Sub-team (where applicable), status (Active, Suspended, Left) and a user page. People shall no longer be referenced as free-text names: every owner, contributor, approver, author, attendee and Role register entry shall link to a User. AI agents are not Users and can never hold an access role or an authority.

Access roles. Access is given by named access roles, each bundling a set of permissions. The framework access roles are Admin, Design Lead, Design Authority, Engineer and Viewer (Annex B.6). Access roles are framework-fixed; a project may not add or edit them, but may grant one-off permission overrides (5A.5).

Project assignment. A User shall have access to a project only through a Project Assignment, which records the project, one access role for that project, the validity dates and who assigned it. A User may hold different access roles on different projects. A User with no active assignment to a project shall not see that project's Production Hub data.

Effectivity access. By default a User shall see every effectivity of each project to which they are assigned. An Admin may restrict a Project Assignment to listed effectivities; the user then sees, filters and edits only data whose effectivity overlaps the allowed effectivities, and the effectivity filter (5.25) offers only those; this applies to both viewing and editing (confirmed by Daniel, 12 Oct 2026). Data with no effectivity (for example EDRs, TSMs and framework pages) is not restricted.

Permission overrides. An Admin may grant or deny a single permission to a User on a project, in addition to the permissions of the access role, with a reason, an expiry date (optional) and the approving Admin recorded. A deny override prevails over the role. Overrides shall be listed on the admin page and on the user page.

Access roles and authority roles. Access roles control what a User may see and edit in the Hub. The authority roles of the Role register (6C.14, Annex B.4) control who may approve, agree, break and release, over a stated area. The two are separate: an authority role assignment shall require an active Project Assignment on that project whose access role includes the matching approval permission (Design Lead access role for a Design Lead authority, Design Authority access role for a Design Authority authority; Admin may hold either). The approval roles Technical Authority for Design, Design Approver and Discipline Lead have no access role of their own and are held on top of the Engineer access role (or Admin). The software shall check both at the date of each decision. Confirmed by Daniel, 12 Oct 2026.

Owner and contributors. Every work item (FDPS, Issue, Action, Lesson Learned, Design Review, Hub Page, Requirement Document, TSM, Verification, Risk and any task record) shall have exactly one accountable Owner, a User, and may have any number of Contributors, also Users. The Owner shall hold an active Project Assignment with edit permission for the item's data type. Ownership changes shall be recorded with who changed it and when. Sub-system and Sub-structure pages keep the derived owner of 5.30 (the Design Lead from the Role register, itself a User).

Admin page. Each Production Hub shall have an admin page, visible only to Users holding the Admin access role on that project, or to a framework administrator, who administers users across all projects (both kept, confirmed by Daniel, 12 Oct 2026), with: a searchable, filterable list of Users (name, Design Team, project, access role, effectivity access, overrides, status, last active); an edit panel per User to add or end Project Assignments, set the access role per project, restrict effectivities, add or remove permission overrides and suspend the User; and an audit trail of every access change. Access changes take effect immediately and are logged as Change Records of type Access change.

User pages. Each User shall have a user page. In this version it shows only the name, Design Team and Sub-team, status, access role per project with effectivity access, authority roles from the Role register, and the items for which the User is Owner or Contributor, grouped by data type. Further content is to be defined.

Permissions. Permissions are per data type and action: View, Create, Edit, Approve (per the authority checks of 6C.14), Release, Administer users. The permission bundle of each access role is set out in Annex B.6.
Annex B.6 access role Admin: Everything an Engineer can do; administer users, Project Assignments, effectivity restrictions and permission overrides on the project (5A.8); view the audit trail.
Annex B.6 access role Design Lead: Engineer permissions; may hold Design Lead authority roles (5A.6); approve EDR line-item breaks and interface breaks within the Role register area.

Annex B.6 access role Design Authority: Engineer permissions; may hold Design Authority authority roles (5A.6); approve TSM statement breaks and bulk-confirm TSM supersessions within the area; approve for release where delegated.

Annex B.6 access role Engineer: View all project data within the allowed effectivities; create and edit FDPSs, line-item reviews, compliance, verifications, issues, actions, lessons and pages they own or contribute to; raise review flags.
Annex B.6 access role Viewer: View only, within the allowed effectivities; may comment and use the AI bar.

records.title: EDRs, line items and link maturity

blocks.text: Requirements are line items grouped into Requirement Documents (EDRs) tagged to Sub-systems; TSMs reach FDPSs through Design Types. Pages above FDPS level list the documents; FDPS pages list each line item with its state. Clauses quoted from Requirements Prompt v24.6.

Level-appropriate display. The information shown on a page shall suit the level of the page. Above FDPS level (Sub-system, System, System Group and Design tree pages above the FDPS), requirement data shall be shown as documents (the applicable EDRs and TSMs, each linking to its own page) and verification data as summaries per document and per FDPS. Only FDPS pages shall list individual EDR line items and TSM statements, with their status (5.27).

EDR and TSM pages. Every EDR and every TSM shall have its own Hub page showing its code, title, issue, tags (Sub-system tags for an EDR; Design Type, Discipline and System tags for a TSM, and the Sub-systems it is reached from), its line items or statements, and the FDPSs inheriting it with a compliance summary.

Page layout. Hub tree pages shall use one layout: a left rail holding the page filters above the collapsible Hub tree, with the current page highlighted, the tree being for quick navigation; a content area that starts with the model preview window at the top left (1.12, 5.16), which can be expanded, beside a generic summary of the node; then all the data of the page in the five page groups of 5.24. The summary shall show what the node is, its status chips, and its structure and parent (parent System and System Group, each a link), its Design Lead as owner (5.30), its Design Sub-team and its permanent ID, each a link to its page or register entry; there shall be no separate Structure and parent category. Summary tiles shall show key counts, each linking to its category and updating with the filters; on a Sub-system page the tiles are FDPS, EDRs, TSMs, Non-compliant, Open Issues and Lessons, with no Part Instances tile.

Page groups and categories. Categories shall be grouped into five page groups, each with its own accessible colour family from the palette (5.28) and shown in a colour key: (a) Requirement (navy #00405E family), on the left: EDRs and TSMs, as documents above FDPS level; (b) Verification (teal #46C1BE family), on the right beside Requirement: Compliance, Verifications and Reviews; (c) Product (neutral grey family), full width below them: on a Sub-system page an FDPSs category only, listing the linked FDPSs, each a link to its FDPS page with a status chip and its Build Stations, and no Part Instances (5.21); (d) Considerations (violet family, light #5B3F8C on #F4F0FA, dark #C7B3EE on #1E1830): Interfacing Systems and Disciplines and Stakeholders; (e) Working Data (amber family, light #7A4E00 on #FBF5E9, dark #F0C674 on #2A2111), at the bottom of the page: Issues and Lessons Learned as separate categories. Every category shall be collapsed by default, with a header showing its name and a count or status chip, and shall expand on selection; an Expand all control shall open or close every category. Selecting or hovering a requirement document shall highlight its compliance and verification rows. There shall be no dedicated Links area: links shall be built into the data, so that every data item that has a page is a link in place (FDPS rows to FDPS pages, EDR and TSM names to their pages, Interfacing Systems to System pages, Issues and Lessons to their records, roles to the Role register, reviews to their Design Reviews, registers from the relevant category), and every page reachable from the former Links list shall stay reachable from the page data, the summary or the tree. On narrow screens the groups shall stack in the order Requirement, Verification, Product, Considerations, Working Data. FDPS pages shall use the same five groups at FDPS level (line items with their status in Requirement, Part Instances in Product); the detailed FDPS page layout is to be confirmed when the FDPS page is designed.

FDPS line items. FDPS pages shall list every inherited EDR line item and TSM statement, grouped by document, with its inheritance route and its status (Inherited, not reviewed; Kept; Broken, with reason and approver; Superseded (auto), with any pending Design Authority bulk confirmation; Direct), and a maturity indicator (line items reviewed of total, counting Kept, Broken and Superseded (auto), and numbers broken and superseded) (6B.7A).

Owner of tree pages. The owner shown on a Sub-system (or Sub-structure) page shall be its Design Lead from the Role register (6C.14), shown as Design Lead (owner); there is no separate owner field for these pages.

Requirement documents. Requirements shall be held as line items grouped into Requirement Documents of kind EDR (Engineering Design Requirements). Every Requirement shall be Part of exactly one EDR. An EDR shall have its own code, title, issue and status, and may cover several Systems (EDRs are intended to be split by System, but overlap is allowed). Each line item shall keep its own level (2C.7), and one EDR may hold line items of different levels.

Allocation. Each EDR shall be tagged at document level to one or more Sub-systems (or Sub-structures); one EDR may be tagged to many Sub-systems and one Sub-system may carry many EDRs. An FDPS shall inherit every EDR tagged to any Sub-system in which at least one of its Part Instances is homed, with all of its line items, by default. A line item may additionally be allocated to one or more nodes of the System tree (a Sub-system, a System or a System Group) as an optional narrowing: where it is, it shall flow only to inheriting FDPSs that have at least one Part Instance homed in a Sub-system at or below an allocated node. Example: a Fuel System usable storage requirement is allocated to the Fuel Storage Sub-system, and every FDPS containing a Part Instance homed in Fuel Storage inherits it. A Requirement may also be linked directly to an FDPS, or to an item for traceability, by a Satisfied by link; the FDPS concerned then holds the Requirement directly.

TSM inheritance. Each TSM shall be tagged with one or more of Design Type, Discipline and System; TSMs shall not be tagged to Sub-systems. Each Sub-system (and Sub-structure) page shall list its applicable Design Types, and a TSM tagged with one of those Design Types shall reach every FDPS with a Part Instance homed in that Sub-system (the route Sub-system > Design Type > TSM). This route is in addition to the matches below. Each kind of tag is optional, but every TSM shall carry at least one tag. A TSM shall reach an FDPS if any one of its tags matches (tags are combined with OR, never AND): a Design Type tag matches when a Part or Assembly in the FDPS's population has that Design Type, including the modification Design Type of a modified bought-in Part (2B.10) and the Design Type Standard Part of catalogue items (1.10.1); a System tag matches when a Part Instance of the FDPS is homed in a Sub-system of that System; and a Discipline tag matches when the Discipline is listed on the Hub page of the FDPS's owning Design Team (the Design Team of its owning Design Sub-team). Matching is never against the Discipline register as a whole, because every Discipline applies to every design (4.2). Where there is doubt, a TSM shall be over-tagged rather than under-tagged. Each Design Team shall list its applicable Design Types and its applicable Disciplines on its Hub page. A Part in an FDPS whose Design Type is not on the owning Design Team's list, or not on the Design Type list of its home Sub-system, shall be flagged. Every matching tag is a basis of the Compliance Statement (6B.6).

Line-item review and breaks. Every line item inherited by an FDPS (each Requirement of an inherited EDR and each statement of an inherited TSM) shall apply by default, with status Inherited, not reviewed. As the design matures, each line item shall be reviewed and either Kept (it applies) or Broken (it does not apply). A break shall record its reason, author, approver and date, and shall be approved under 6C.13. The inheritance shall not be deleted: a Broken line item stays visible and shall be flagged for re-confirmation when the FDPS population, its lead Sub-system, the document's tags or the line item itself change. A Requirement or TSM all of whose line items are Broken does not apply to the FDPS. Directly linked Requirements (6B.2) are shown as Direct alongside their status. Once the FDPS has defined links for a document, 6B.7A applies.

Link maturity: flow down, define, flow up and supersede. Early, high-level links (EDRs tagged to Sub-systems, 6B.2; TSMs reached through Design Types, 6B.5) let work be linked before it is defined, and flow DOWN to every FDPS below as inherited line items (6B.7). As the design matures and Part Instances are known, defined links shall be made at the lowest level (to Part Instances or Assembly Instances); defined links flow back UP and SUPERSEDE the flowed-down links. Once a level has defined links (P2 below), every flowed-down line item of that document in that FDPS that no defined link reaches shall be superseded AUTOMATICALLY, with status Superseded (auto), and no manual break is needed. Superseded EDR line items need no confirmation. Superseded TSM statements shall require a BULK confirmation by the Design Authority (6C.13) for each FDPS and TSM; until confirmed they are shown as Superseded (auto), pending confirmation. Before a level has defined links, line items may still be Kept or Broken manually under 6B.7, a break still requiring reason and approver. For the gates (6C.11, 6C.15), Kept, Broken and Superseded (auto) line items count as reviewed; a pending Design Authority bulk confirmation of TSM supersessions blocks both gates.

Change flags. Line items shall carry their own revisions. A new issue of an EDR or TSM shall flag, for every inheriting FDPS, only the line items that changed, were added or were removed in that issue, together with their Compliance Statements and Kept or Broken status; unchanged line items keep their status. Added line items arrive as Inherited, not reviewed. A changed item, revision or Verification shall flag the Compliance Statements whose evidence it affects.
